keyFindings.finding: Method for honest dollar conversion: (1) Convert each rupee amount at the average rate for the year it was spent, giving 'then-dollars'. (2) Bring that figure up to today's dollars with the US CPI-U, for example with the BLS CPI Inflation Calculator. (3) Disclose the method once on screen. Do not use today's rate on a 1990s rupee amount, because that badly understates what the money was worth then. Note that 'adjust by Indian inflation, then convert' and 'convert, then adjust by US inflation' give different answers. Pick one method, use it throughout, and say which one it is.

keyFindings.finding: Framing for US viewers (editorial guidance): present the story as a small-business, self-made story that Americans already know (a family shop that outgrew itself, a first van bought on borrowed money, still doing his original trade). Do not frame it as an immigrant story; he built the business in Bengaluru. Use Bengaluru's role as India's tech hub to explain why corporate clients needed cars, without turning the city into backdrop scenery. Avoid: making India look exotic (snake-charmer or slum stock shots, sitar clichés), poverty porn (lingering on hardship for shock), accent or name jokes, 'even an Indian barber...' condescension, and presenting him as a curiosity rather than a businessman. Give his own words through subtitles or a respectful voiceover, never a put-on accent.
keyFindings.evidence: Editorial recommendation based on general knowledge, not on a cited audience study. No source was fetched.

keyFindings.finding: US defamation basics for profiling a living, semi-public person (not legal advice; have a lawyer review). Truth is a defense, and opinion clearly presented as opinion is generally protected. Public officials and public figures must prove 'actual malice' (New York Times v. Sullivan, 1964). For private figures, states may set a lower standard such as negligence (Gertz v. Robert Welch, 1974). A businessman who has given many media interviews about his rise may count as a 'limited-purpose public figure' for that story; that is a legal judgment call. Also watch for: false light (true footage edited to imply something false), and using his likeness in thumbnails or ads in a way that implies he endorses the channel. Never state numbers such as net worth or fleet value as fact unless they are sourced. Attribute them ('he told [outlet] in [year]...'). He lives in India, so Indian defamation law may also apply. That is outside this US brief.
keyFindings.evidence: General legal knowledge; case names and years are from memory and were not checked against a source in this run.

keyFindings.finding: FTC and YouTube disclosure: these apply only if the video has sponsorship, affiliate links or free products. If so, the FTC Endorsement Guides require a clear disclosure in the video itself, and YouTube requires ticking its 'paid promotion' setting. If AI-generated or realistic synthetic re-enactments or voices are used, YouTube's altered or synthetic content disclosure setting applies. Licensed real footage needs no FTC disclosure, but keep license records in case of Content ID disputes.
keyFindings.evidence: General knowledge of FTC and YouTube policies; ftc.gov was unreachable (ENOTFOUND) and no YouTube help page was fetched.

keyFindings.finding: US YouTube norms for a 45-minute documentary (no audience data gathered).
